vignette:
Malia was 31 years old, a married dancer of Pacific Islander heritage, and when she first came to treatment she spoke about the past in the careful, measured way of someone who had learned early to keep her voice steady. As a child, she had witnessed repeated domestic violence between two adults she trusted, and what stayed with her most was not one single scene but the shock of realizing that the home she depended on could suddenly become unsafe. She remembered the sound of raised voices, the momentary stillness before things escalated, and the way she would stand frozen in place, trying to make herself small and unnoticed. Even now, she described the original event as something that had left her with the lasting sense that a person could be violated by someone they depended on most.

As she grew older, reminders began to arrive in ordinary, humiliating ways. Hearing names that sounded like those from the family members involved in the violence could instantly pull her back into the old terror, even if the person speaking had meant nothing by it. In those moments she would feel a sharp tightening in her chest and become acutely aware of her own heart racing or pounding, as though her body were already preparing for danger before her mind had fully caught up. She was especially unsettled when she felt watched or observed. In rehearsals, in mirrors, or even when crossing a room in her studio, she would suddenly become convinced that other people's eyes were fixed on her in a way that was not neutral, and that familiar sensation could make her want to turn away or leave. These experiences were not limited to any one setting; she said that something in her surroundings could bring back the full memory without warning, sometimes a tone of voice, sometimes a name, sometimes the abrupt awareness of a silence in the room, and she would be taken back to the scene so quickly that it felt less like remembering than being dropped into it.

When Malia recalled what had happened, shame was often the first feeling that rose. She spoke with visible discomfort about how intensely ashamed she felt when the memory came up, as though her body remembered something unforgivable. At other times she could describe the event with a flat, disconnected quality, saying that she could remember what happened but feel completely numb, as if it had happened to a stranger. That emotional distance did not make the memory easier; instead, it left her unsettled by how familiar and unreal it could feel at the same time. She was especially troubled by the meaning she had come to attach to it. She had come to believe that she had been betrayed by someone she trusted, and that there was something about her that made the event happen. Alongside that, she had grown increasingly convinced that people are not what they seem. She did not describe this as a dramatic suspicion so much as a hard-earned caution, a way of moving through the world that made it difficult to relax fully around others, even those she loved.

These experiences had gradually shaped her daily life and work. As a dancer, Malia spent much of her time in studios with mirrors, instructors, and other bodies moving around her, and the feeling of being watched could appear there with particular force. She found herself scanning faces, watching for shifts in attention, and becoming tense when someone commented on her form or called her name across the room. Though she remained committed to her work, she noticed that these moments made it harder to stay present in rehearsal and left her feeling exposed in spaces that once held meaning for her. At home, too, her marriage had become the place where her vigilance was most visible. She cared deeply for her husband, but she also noticed that trust did not come easily when he or anyone else seemed too certain, too close, or too quick to read her. Over time, the strain of holding these reactions in silence wore on her, and what finally brought her to seek help was the sense that the memories and reminders were becoming harder to manage without withdrawing from the people and places that mattered to her. She came hoping for relief from the sudden flooding of the past, and what she feared most was that she would continue to carry shame, suspicion, and the feeling of being watched everywhere she went.
